issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'full sensory reliving' suggests highly vivid, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which sits in marked tension with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' Those two can sometimes coexist, but as a three-item profile with shame on recall they pull in opposing directions and are clinically questionable together.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'Avoid enclosed spaces' is not clearly coherent with the rest of the profile for sexual assault as described here. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, delays, shame, and vivid reliving; enclosed spaces introduces a more specific situational avoidance that is not supported by the memory/threat content and looks disconnected from the formulation, especially since Triggers is not active in this case.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'When I remember the event I feel intense shame' and 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time.' Severe shame and terror on recall usually make disclosure difficult rather than easy, so this combination is clinically questionable within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Ruminate about how to get even with assailant' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile for this trauma type and patient presentation. The Memory and Threat items emphasize shame, terror, hypervigilance, and avoidance, which is more consistent with fear-based post-assault PTSD; revenge-focused rumination pulls toward a different emotional/cognitive stance and lacks support elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the rest of the presentation. The dominant active formulation is Memory↔Threat↔Maladaptive Strategies around trauma recollection and danger monitoring after sexual assault; gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is too nonspecific and does not connect clearly to the patient's other selected threat and memory items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Enclosed Spaces' appears to be a trigger/avoidance cue rather than a maladaptive strategy, and it is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, shame, terror, and speechless recall; avoidance of enclosed spaces is a different contextual pattern that is not otherwise supported here.

vignette:
Mark has been a social worker for nearly thirty years, a career built on his capacity to enter chaotic situations and find a path forward. Now, at fifty-three, he finds his own world has become the one he can no longer navigate. The change began eight months ago, following a home visit to a new client. He remembers waiting in the narrow, dim apartment hallway, a delay that felt unusual at the time but now replays in his mind as a premonition. When the door finally opened, he was pulled inside. The assault happened quickly, brutally, in a small, cluttered bedroom with the door shut. The feeling of being overpowered in that confined space, the door a barrier to any possible escape, is the memory that has since dismantled his life.

In the weeks that followed, the event lived not as a coherent story but as a series of punishing sensory fragments. When he tries to remember it, to make sense of what happened, the same suffocating terror he felt in that room returns, a physical wave of cold dread that steals his breath. He has tried, on several occasions, to explain it to his wife, Sarah, but the words refuse to form. He knows what happened, he can see it behind his eyes, but language fails him. The attempt itself brings on an intense, hot shame that silences him completely, leaving him feeling hollowed out and pathetic. He has come to believe that being unable to speak about it is a profound personal failing, another layer of weakness.

His daily routines are now governed by a constant, humming sense of threat. Walking from his office to the parking garage has become a tactical mission. He is acutely aware of every person behind him, the sound of their footsteps seeming to quicken with his own. He finds himself stopping abruptly to pretend to tie a shoe or check his phone, just for the chance to look over his shoulder and confirm no one is following him. Unfamiliar places have become impossible. At work, he refuses any new cases that would require a home visit in a part of the city he doesn't know well. He tells his supervisor it's a matter of efficiency, but in truth, he cannot bear the thought of walking into a building where he can't anticipate the dangers. This has created a noticeable friction with his colleagues and a growing file of deferred cases on his desk.

To manage the intrusive memories, Mark has developed strategies that only seem to dig him deeper into his distress. He spends hours at night, long after Sarah is asleep, ruminating. He replays the assault not as it was, but as it could have been. In these fantasies, he is not frozen; he fights back, he overpowers his assailant, he escapes. He imagines tracking the man down, exacting a cold and satisfying revenge. These thoughts provide a fleeting sense of control, but they are exhausting and always leave him feeling more helpless than before. When the memories or the rage become too overwhelming, he tries to shove them down, to force them out of his mind by focusing intently on paperwork or a television show, but it's like holding a beach ball underwater; the thoughts always surge back with greater force.

The world feels like it is closing in on him. He takes the stairs at his office building now, unable to tolerate the few seconds inside a sealed elevator. He feels a spike of panic in small, windowless meeting rooms. His marriage is strained by his silence, and his job, the bedrock of his identity, is becoming precarious. It was a final warning from his supervisor about his "unwillingness to engage with new client populations" that finally propelled him to seek help. He is terrified of losing his career, but what frightens him more is the chilling realization that he is losing himself. He has come to therapy with the fragile hope of finding the words he has lost, and perhaps, a way back to the man he used to be.
